$comment: Every way the TypeScript ops and the Python MCP server disagree about which tools exist, what parameters they take and whether they change anything -- one entry each. Result shapes, runtime guards, wording, value constraints, what is inside an object, whether a tool accepts parameters it does not declare (Python closes its schemas with additionalProperties false, the ops say nothing) and every annotation but the read-only hint are outside what the check compares, so they never show up here: a difference can be real and still have no entry, and list_pages carrying no total_matches on the TypeScript side is the standing example. What the check will not do is summarize a construct nobody taught it: it follows no references at all, and a $ref, a $defs, a keyword at the top of an input schema it cannot read, or a composition it does not model stops the run instead of quietly comparing what is left. The parity test fails on a divergence that is not listed here and on a listing the two surfaces no longer support, so this file is the TypeScript to-do list and cannot quietly rot. An entry records that a difference is KNOWN, not that it is fine -- read the status. Statuses: intentional (settled, will not change), pending-port (somebody has read both sides and a TS-side change is owed -- a whole op, or something an existing op still lacks), pending-decision (waiting on a call nobody has made), unreviewed-gap (found by the comparator, nobody has ruled on it yet). What separates pending-port from unreviewed-gap is whether anyone has read both sides, not how serious the difference is: several unreviewed-gap entries describe the same undeclared-default problem as the pending-port ones.

snakeCaseParamNames.reason: TS ops take camelCase parameters on the wire, Python snake_case. Which one wins is an open decision, so the comparator folds the two spellings together rather than listing every parameter on the surface as a divergence. Set this to false once the decision lands and the losing side has been renamed.

pythonNullDefaults.reason: `x: str | None = None` is how Python spells an optional parameter; the null default carries nothing the TS `.optional()` does not already say.

optionalNullUnions.reason: An OPTIONAL Python parameter typed `T | None` is compared as plain `T`, because that union is how Python spells optional and requiredness is compared separately. A nullable parameter that is required keeps its null, where the union really is part of the contract.

ratchet.$comment: unreviewed-gap is the one status nobody has ruled on, so it is the one meant to go only down. This number is how many of them the registry is allowed to hold: the check fails when there are more, and fails asking for this number to come down when there are fewer, so the count and the number cannot drift apart. What no check can do is stop somebody raising both together -- that edit is in the diff, and refusing it is a reviewer's job. A gap found from here on wants a status somebody reviewed and a reason, not a bigger number.

divergences.observed: python=write (tag) params=[api_key type=string required=false default=none; url type=string required=false default=none]
divergences.reason: TS takes the Galaxy URL and key when the server is built, so there is no per-session connect call to expose.

The paged-listing convention above. Python's data is bioblend's return value, which the manifest generator cannot read, so only the TS side states a kind; the difference is the wrapper, not the rows.

The TS name for Python's `contents`; see that entry.
The window inside the data, which the paged-listing convention above decides. Both surfaces also report it in the envelope.

Both surfaces page this listing and disagree about what `data` is: Python puts the rows there and the window beside them, the TS op puts `{items, pagination}` there and the window beside that as well. An agent reading `data` gets rows on one surface and a wrapper on the other. Which convention is right is one decision for every paged op, recorded here so it is made from the whole list rather than one tool at a time.
The TS spelling of Python's unsupported_tools; see that entry.
The same list under two names: Python calls it unsupported_tools, the TS op unsupported_ops. One name has to win and neither surface is obviously the reference for it.
Where the enforced version came from, which the TS op reports and Python does not. Useful or noise is a decision; it is not a port either way.
